sixpence.name: Sixpence
sixpence.description: Tilly, by the fountain in Castle square, has lost her black cat. He hasn't come in since Sunday. She thinks he's in the churchyard behind the church, where she isn't allowed to go.
sixpence.completion: Tilly's cat was on the new stone in the churchyard, the one with a date and no name. He let me pick him up. He was cold right through, and he stayed cold against me all the way back to the square. Tilly said Mum says he's always cold now, and put him inside her coat.

requirements.text: Sixpence, in the churchyard behind the church

sixpence.returnTo: Tilly, by the fountain in Castle square

second_post.name: Second Post
second_post.description: Miss Dray, outside the Post Office on Castle square, has three letters with the wrong numbers on them. They go through three doors in town: the Forge, No. 4 Back Lane, and the Doctor's. She said nobody will answer.
second_post.completion: A letter through each door. Nobody came to any of them. Miss Dray gave me a key that came to her office with no name on it, and said she sorts by street and this one has no street.

requirements.text: A letter to the Forge, on Cross Lane
A letter to No. 4, Back Lane
A letter to the Doctor's, on Pound Lane

second_post.returnTo: Miss Dray, outside the Post Office on Castle square

washing_day.name: Washing Day
washing_day.description: Mrs Marsh, at her line in front of No. 5 High Street, lost three things off it on a day with no wind. One is by the church door, one by the fountain, and one in the yard of the Castle Arms.
washing_day.completion: A pillowcase, a shirt and a sheet, each one folded. Mrs Marsh said she hadn't folded them. She gave me two vials of pump water.

requirements.text: Washing, by the church, the fountain and the Arms yard

washing_day.returnTo: Mrs Marsh, at her washing line on the High Street

the_last_name.name: The Last Name
the_last_name.description: Mr Hale, the smith, outside the Forge on Cross Lane, wants the last name on the memorial in Castle square read out to him. He told me his eyes are good. He'd rather not be the one who reads it.
the_last_name.completion: HALE, R. I read it out to him. He said it back the way a man checks a delivery, twice, and gave me two bars of iron from under his bench.

requirements.text: The last name on the memorial, in Castle square

the_last_name.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

roberts_cap.name: Robert's Cap
roberts_cap.description: Mr Hale says his boy Robert has been up in his room over the Forge since the bell. He wants somebody to knock and tell him his tea is on. He wouldn't say why he won't go up himself.
roberts_cap.completion: Nobody on the stairs, and a cap on the peg inside the Forge door. I took it down to Mr Hale. He turned it over in his hands, then gave it back to me to hold.

requirements.text: Robert's cap, on the peg inside the Forge door

roberts_cap.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

the_new_stone.name: The New Stone
the_new_stone.description: There's a new stone in the churchyard behind the church, with a date on it and no name. Mr Hale wants Robert's cap left on it. He said he'll cut the name himself when his hands are ready.
the_new_stone.completion: I left the cap on the new stone. Mr Hale said he'd thought the date was for him. The forge was lit when I got back, and he gave me a stone from it that keeps its heat.

requirements.text: The new stone in the churchyard, behind the church

the_new_stone.returnTo: the smith, Mr Hale, outside the Forge on Cross Lane

on_the_hour.name: On the Hour
on_the_hour.description: Mr Dunn, by the telephone box in Castle square, is waiting for his brother to ring. It rang once last week and he couldn't make it out. He asked me, being younger, to lift the receiver and listen.
on_the_hour.completion: A man's voice, a long way off: tell Walter he's at the Arms, and to come before the lamps. Then the line went. I told Mr Dunn. He said his brother has never been in a public house in his life.

requirements.text: The telephone box in Castle square

on_the_hour.returnTo: the telephone box in Castle square, and Mr Dunn

the_back_room.name: The Back Room
the_back_room.description: Mr Dunn is chapel and doesn't go into the Castle Arms. He asked me to find Mrs Garland, who keeps the bar, and ask whether his brother Ernest has been in.
the_back_room.completion: Mrs Garland said Ernest took the back room in the spring, the night of the bell, and hasn't come down since. She leaves his tray at the door. I told Mr Dunn. He's stopped watching the telephone box and watches the door of the Arms instead.

requirements.text: Mrs Garland, inside the Castle Arms

the_back_room.returnTo: the telephone box in Castle square, and Mr Dunn

the_fourth_lane.name: The Fourth Lane
the_fourth_lane.description: Dot, on Cross Lane, is counting the lanes of Castle. She's got three and is sure there used to be four. She wants the name signs read to her. They all stand at the west end of the town, where she isn't allowed.
the_fourth_lane.completion: Back Lane, Cross Lane, Pound Lane. Three. Dot didn't say anything for a bit, then gave me a nasturtium she'd taken off Mrs Crewe's stall when nobody was looking.

requirements.text: The Back Lane sign, at the west end of Back Lane
The Cross Lane sign, at the west end of Cross Lane
The Pound Lane sign, at the west end of Pound Lane

school_lane.name: School Lane
school_lane.description: Dot says the lane that runs up past the church to the north gate has no name anywhere in town, and nobody walks up it. There's a sign at the top. Her mum won't take her.
school_lane.completion: CHURCH LANE, and under the paint, SCHOOL LANE. I told Dot. She said that was the fourth, and that they don't say it any more. She gave me a key she'd found in the gutter.

requirements.text: The sign at the end of Church Lane, by the north gate

two_loaves.name: Two Loaves
two_loaves.description: Mrs Oddie, at the bread stall in Castle square, bakes for forty. No. 7 Pound Lane had two loaves every morning, and nobody has been up for them in a fortnight. She asked me to leave one on their step.
two_loaves.completion: I left the loaf on the step of No. 7. The curtain moved to the edge and stopped. Mrs Oddie said they never take it in while there's anyone to see.

requirements.text: A loaf for No. 7, Pound Lane

two_loaves.returnTo: Mrs Oddie, at the bread stall in Castle square

paid_to_sunday.name: Paid to Sunday
paid_to_sunday.description: The Milkman leaves No. 7 its milk every morning and nobody takes it in. He asked me to lift the bottles inside the door. There was always money on the mat, he said. He's on his round behind Pound Lane from seven to nine in the morning.
paid_to_sunday.completion: The hall swept, Mrs Oddie's loaf on the table untouched, and the milk money counted out on the mat. I told the Milkman. He counted it and said it was paid to Sunday, same as last week.

requirements.text: The milk on the step of No. 7, Pound Lane

paid_to_sunday.returnTo: the Milkman, on his round behind Pound Lane, seven to nine

never_any_eggs.name: Never Any Eggs
never_any_eggs.description: Mrs Bex comes to the market in Castle square for eggs, and there are never any. She asked me to look in the hen house behind Pound Lane, past the green. She's stopped going to look herself.
never_any_eggs.completion: Three eggs in the straw, and a card propped behind them with her name on it in her own hand. Mrs Bex looked at it a while. She didn't remember writing it. She gave me grapes, because she'd bought too many again.

requirements.text: The hen house behind Pound Lane

never_any_eggs.returnTo: Mrs Bex, at the market in Castle square

white_roses.name: White Roses
white_roses.description: Mr Sallis, in the garden of No. 1 High Street, wants one of his roses taken to his wife Edith. She's in the churchyard behind the church, the first stone inside the gate off the lane. He doesn't go in.
white_roses.completion: Under the rose I left there were others, dried brown, one for every week. I counted them. Mr Sallis said he hasn't been in since the funeral. He gave me pansies off the bed by his gate.

requirements.text: Edith Sallis's stone, in the churchyard behind the church

white_roses.returnTo: the garden of No. 1, High Street, and Mr Sallis

the_constables_paces.name: A Hundred and Twelve
the_constables_paces.description: The Constable walks the High Street end to end and says it's two paces longer than when he started. He asked me to walk it too: from the lamps at the west end to the lamps at the east.
the_constables_paces.completion: I'd counted without meaning to: a hundred and fourteen. I told the Constable. He wrote it in his book and didn't say anything.

requirements.text: The lamps at the west end of the High Street
The lamps at the east end of the High Street

the_constables_paces.returnTo: the Constable, walking the High Street

too_red.name: Too Red
too_red.description: Mrs Hobb, in the garden of No. 7 High Street, wants two apples from the orchard behind the house taken to Mr Tolly, on the bench by the memorial in Castle square. She says he won't pick them himself. He says they're too red this year.
too_red.completion: Mr Tolly held one up to the light and said it was redder than last year. Then he ate it.

requirements.text: Two apples, from the orchard behind No. 7, High Street

too_red.returnTo: the bench by the memorial in Castle square, and Mr Tolly
